title: Building Reliability Into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover
gist: A practitioner account of an intermittent AWS S3 change that broke Terraform registry downloads (via go-getter HEAD requests on signed URLs) and took nearly 24 hours to resolve, used to argue that cloud SLAs are statistical, observability must act as a control plane (detect-act-confirm with Prometheus, Route 53 and Lambda), active-active beats untested passive regions, and DNS TTL and shallow health checks routinely defeat failover.

insights.claim: An AWS S3 internal deployment changed how HEAD requests on signed URLs were handled, causing intermittent 404s when HashiCorp's go-getter library (used by Terraform for module downloads) issued a HEAD before each GET under concurrent load, breaking an S3-backed Terraform registry until AWS rolled the change back.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Even top-tier managed services ship regressions that surface only in specific client call patterns; concentration on a single provider's primitive is a hidden systemic risk.
insights.locator: We found the real cause by building a controlled test environment

insights.claim: In the S3 signed-URL incident, detection took a few hours but recovery took nearly twenty-four hours, mostly spent on support calls proving the issue was AWS's and waiting for acknowledgment and rollback, with AWS support initially not recognizing the hypothesis.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Vendor-side recovery time, not detection, dominates outage duration for managed dependencies, which customers cannot control.
insights.locator: Detection took a few hours. Recovery took nearly twenty-four hours

insights.claim: When a managed dependency fails intermittently, engineers should reproduce the client's exact call pattern outside production and instrument the client rather than only the server; a load test reproduced the S3 failure within ten minutes.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Practical debugging pattern that shortens time-to-root-cause with cloud vendors.
insights.locator: The lesson I took from this situation

insights.claim: A 99.99 percent SLA allows about fifty-two minutes and thirty-six seconds of downtime per year and is a statistical claim about a distribution, so at sufficient scale systems will eventually hit its tail and must be designed for it.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Investors and operators should treat cloud SLAs as probabilistic and value multi-region resilience tooling accordingly.
insights.quote: A 99.99 percent SLA is a statistic, not a promise.

insights.claim: The core observability mistake is treating it as a reporting layer to inform humans rather than a control plane that evaluates signals against policy, acts automatically and then informs humans; the human-in-the-loop model scales only with headcount and on-call capacity.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Favors vendors that close the loop from monitoring to automated remediation over pure dashboarding.
insights.quote: An alert that wakes a human only speeds up notification.
insights.locator: The mistake has nothing to do with tooling choice

insights.claim: Observability stacks such as Prometheus and Grafana decay as expertise concentrates and original authors leave, so alerts drift out of calibration; they need the same ownership model as production services, with regular reviews, failure testing and collective ownership.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Hidden operational cost of self-run open-source observability supports demand for managed observability offerings.
insights.locator: I have run Prometheus and Grafana stacks

insights.claim: A reliable automated DR loop chains a composite Prometheus alert (e.g. 5xx rate above 3% AND p99 latency above 800ms sustained for 90 seconds, evaluated per region) to Route 53 weighted routing or an Alertmanager-webhook-triggered Lambda failover, then a confirmation Lambda that polls the target region's health until healthy before notifying humans, with an unconfirmed result itself becoming an alert.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Reference architecture for detect-act-confirm; composite, duration-gated signals reduce false-positive failovers.
insights.locator: The pattern looks like this in practice

insights.claim: Most DR implementations have detection, fewer have an automated response layer, and fewer still have a confirmation layer verifying the response worked; automated failover without confirmation is an untested hypothesis.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Gap in most enterprises' resilience posture, an opportunity for resilience and chaos-engineering tooling.
insights.quote: Faster detection only sharpens the post-mortem timeline.
insights.locator: What separates DR systems that actually work

insights.claim: A passive region that has never carried production traffic accumulates configuration drift, cold caches and unexercised dependencies, so active-active (run 50/50 normally, 100/0 under failure, validated with chaos tests) is preferable for critical dependencies despite higher cost and sync complexity.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Active-active roughly doubles steady-state infrastructure footprint for critical services, supporting cloud consumption.
insights.quote: A passive region that has never carried production traffic is an untested hypothesis.

insights.claim: Regional failover cannot fix a non-regional failure: the S3 incident hit both regions simultaneously, so automation would bounce traffic between two broken regions, and Route 53 returns all weighted records when all are unhealthy; the correct response to simultaneous degradation is to hold traffic and page a human.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Multi-region on one cloud does not hedge shared-service failures; correlated provider risk persists.
insights.locator: Two failure modes in this design

insights.claim: Shallow /health endpoints that only confirm the process is running will keep returning 200 when a regional database is down, causing Route 53 and confirmation checks to keep routing to a broken region; health checks must exercise real functionality, such as a lightweight database read, without depending on resources shared across regions.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: A common failure point in otherwise well-designed DR setups.
insights.locator: The second failure mode is a health check

insights.claim: DNS TTL is the most common DR misconfiguration: a high TTL (often an IaC module default of 300-600 seconds) leaves clients hitting a degraded region after a correct failover, while a too-low TTL causes flip-flopping on transient spikes; it must be chosen against RTO, health-check interval and false-positive tolerance.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Cheap configuration fix with outsized impact on effective recovery time.
insights.quote: DNS TTL can nullify a perfectly executed failover.
insights.locator: DNS TTL is the single most common DR misconfiguration

insights.claim: Game days that inject real failures into production expose human gaps such as unclear decision authority and missing runbooks, and teams most often skip testing whether the confirmation layer correctly recognizes a successful failover and stops acting, a path to self-inflicted cascading failures.
insights.speaker: Saurabh Ahuja
insights.so_what: Points to demand for structured chaos and game-day tooling.
insights.locator: The validation that teams most consistently skip
